learn: Observational drawing trains you to draw what you see rather than what you know.
Use contour, blind contour and gesture exercises to warm up.
Measure with sighting and check proportions constantly.
check: Blind contour means looking only at the...
lessons.try: Do three warm-up drawings of the same object using different methods.

learn: Arrange objects with varied shapes, textures and reflective surfaces.
Establish composition, then block in shapes, then develop values and details.
Reflective objects show distorted reflections and strong highlights.
lessons.try: Draw a still life including glass or metal.

learn: Draw interior and exterior spaces from life.
Simplify complex scenes into big shapes.
Use value to separate foreground, middle ground and background.
lessons.try: Draw a view through a window from observation.

learn: One-point: one vanishing point, for scenes viewed straight on.
Two-point: two vanishing points, for objects viewed from a corner.
All vanishing points lie on the horizon line, at eye level.
lessons.try: Draw a street corner in two-point perspective.

learn: Adds a third vanishing point above or below the horizon.
Used for dramatic views of tall buildings or from above.
Vertical lines converge toward the third point.
check: Three-point perspective adds a vanishing point...
lessons.try: Draw a skyscraper from a worm's-eye view.

learn: Circles in perspective become ellipses.
Figures in a scene shrink toward the horizon; their eyes stay near the horizon line if standing on the same ground.
Use perspective grids to place figures correctly.
check: Standing figures' eyes stay near the...
lessons.try: Draw a street scene with people at different distances.

learn: Mix colours from a limited palette: a warm and cool version of each primary.
Mixing complements makes neutral greys and browns.
Test mixes on scrap paper before painting.
check: A limited palette uses a warm and cool of each...
lessons.try: Mix a twelve-step colour wheel from a limited palette.

learn: Warm light creates cool shadows; cool light creates warm shadows.
Atmospheric perspective makes distant colours cooler and less saturated.
Impressionists observed coloured shadows outdoors.
lessons.try: Paint the same object in warm and cool light.

learn: Expressionist colour exaggerates for emotion rather than accuracy.
The Fauves ("wild beasts") like Henri Matisse used bold, unnatural colour around 1905.
Choose a colour scheme to match the mood of your concept.
lessons.try: Paint a portrait using expressive, non-realistic colour.

learn: An underpainting establishes values in a single colour.
Build layers from thin to thick and dark to light in opaque media.
Glazes are transparent layers that alter colour.
lessons.try: Paint a still life with a monochrome underpainting.

learn: Brushwork can be smooth and invisible or expressive and textured.
Alla prima ("at first attempt") paints wet-into-wet in one session.
Palette knives create bold textures.
lessons.try: Paint a landscape alla prima in one session.

learn: Painting from life captures true colour and light.
Photos flatten space and distort colour; use them as references, not copies.
Use only photos you took or have permission to use.
check: Took or have permission to use
lessons.try: Paint a landscape from life, then one from your own photo; compare.

learn: Linocut and woodcut remove areas that will not print.
Plan reversal: images print as mirror images.
Cut safely away from the body with a bench hook.
lessons.try: Carve and print a linocut in black on white.

learn: Intaglio holds ink in lines below the surface; drypoint scratches directly into a plate.
Collagraphs build a textured plate from glued materials.
Both require pressure from a press or careful burnishing.
lessons.try: Make a collagraph plate from cardboard and textured materials.

learn: Multi-block or reduction printing builds colour layers.
Registration aligns each colour.
Number, title and sign editions in pencil.
lessons.try: Make a two-colour print with accurate registration.

learn: Sculpture works with positive form and negative space.
Consider how a sculpture looks from every angle.
Barbara Hepworth and Henry Moore used holes to make space part of the form.
check: Holes in sculpture make ___ part of the form.
lessons.try: Make a small sculpture where negative space is important.

learn: Additive: clay, wire, papier-mâché, assemblage. Subtractive: carving plaster, soap or wood.
Armatures support additive sculptures.
Work safely with tools and materials.
lessons.try: Build a wire armature and cover it with papier-mâché.

learn: 3D design includes product, furniture and architectural models.
Prototypes test form, function and materials.
Design for the user: comfort, safety, beauty.
lessons.try: Design and build a model of a chair.

learn: Renaissance art (1400s-1500s) revived classical ideals with perspective, anatomy and humanism.
Leonardo's "The Last Supper", Michelangelo's "David" and Raphael's "School of Athens".
Northern Renaissance artists like Jan van Eyck developed oil painting detail.
check: Jan van Eyck was a ___ Renaissance artist.
lessons.try: Compare an Italian and a Northern Renaissance painting.

learn: Baroque (1600s): drama and movement (Caravaggio, Rubens, Rembrandt).
Rococo (1700s): light, playful, decorative (Fragonard).
Neoclassicism (late 1700s): order and virtue inspired by Greece and Rome (Jacques-Louis David).
lessons.try: Make a chart comparing the three styles.

learn: Romanticism (early 1800s) emphasised emotion and nature (Turner, Delacroix).
Realism (mid-1800s) showed ordinary life (Courbet, Millet).
Impressionism (1870s) captured light and moments (Monet, Renoir, Morisot, Degas).
lessons.try: Paint a scene in the Impressionist manner outdoors.

learn: Post-Impressionism (Van Gogh, Cézanne, Gauguin) led to modern art.
Cubism (Picasso, Braque) fragmented form; Futurism celebrated speed.
Dada questioned what counts as art after World War I.
lessons.try: Make a cubist still life collage.

learn: Abstract Expressionism (1940s-1950s) used gesture and colour fields.
Pop Art (1960s) drew from advertising and mass culture.
Minimalism reduced art to simple geometric forms.
lessons.try: Make a Pop Art-style print of an everyday object.

learn: Contemporary art (since about 1970) includes installation, performance, video, digital and socially engaged art.
Artists explore identity, environment, technology and history.
Context and concept are often as important as materials.
lessons.try: Propose a contemporary artwork about an issue you care about.

learn: Graphic design uses hierarchy, alignment, contrast, repetition and proximity.
Grids organise layouts.
White space improves clarity.
lessons.try: Redesign a cluttered flyer using design principles.

learn: Typefaces: serif, sans-serif, script, display.
Kerning adjusts space between letters; leading adjusts space between lines.
Limit typefaces to two or three per design.
lessons.try: Design a poster using only typography.

learn: A brand identity includes logo, colours and typography.
Logos should be simple, memorable and scalable.
Designers research audience and purpose first.
lessons.try: Design a logo and brand guide for an imaginary café.

learn: Describe, analyse, interpret, evaluate.
Use art vocabulary and specific references.
Balance strengths and suggestions.
lessons.try: Lead a critique of a classmate's work.

learn: Explain what the work is, how you made it and why.
Mention influences and the concept.
Keep it clear and personal.
lessons.try: Write artist statements for three works.

learn: Select a cohesive body of work showing growth and range.
Document work with good photographs.
Include sketchbook pages to show process.
lessons.try: Assemble a portfolio of twelve works with statements.
